This project had two primary objectives. Firstly, to develop a sophisticated numerical model that accurately predicts the formation and properties of the modulator's primary output, including its temporal evolution, spatial distribution, and correlation with other phenomena like phonon poisson's spots and sound holes. Secondly, based on this computational model, to design an experimental approach that can effectively utilize the modulator's primary output to gain precise insights into the acoustic field's wavevector. This has practical implications for the measurement of acoustic wavevector since most existing methods rely on poorly resolved interferograms in a single wavelength. By combining numerical simulation and experimental techniques, we found that the correlation of the electrooptic and acoustic signals from two crossed AOMs, which are identified in a 2D map, can determine the modulus of the acoustic wavevector. This knowledge was then used to measure the wavevector associated with a 1.03 $\mu$m wavelength laser, yielding a value of 282.83 m^-1. Furthermore, we found that the modulator's primary output can be optimized by adjusting several variables including the laser's frequency, power, and trajectory as well as the crystal's orientation, allowing us to enhance its signal by a factor of 10. Lastly, we proposed an improved version of the modulator, which incorporates the benefits of both the defocusing and the f-f Raman nuclei interactions to increase its acoustic field's wavevector resolution from 1 % to 0.1 % while maintaining the same signal to noise ratio. This research will be beneficial to a broad range of scientists, who utilize AOMs as a fundamental tool in their respective fields including nonlinear optics, quantum physics, deep learning, and biophotonics. Several key techniques such as optical trapping, coherent control of atoms and molecules, and the manipulation of light waves will significantly benefit from the findings of this study. web page structure poses a major issue for automated web exploration. This limitation is exacerbated when users employ features like tabs or groupings to organize their browsing experience. Manually reconstructing the user-perceived structure of web pages is impractical due to their dynamic nature and the need for accurate manual reorganization. This research presents a novel method utilizing minimal human intervention to streamline creating user-perceived web page structures. Our approach employs visual structure manipulation through logical elimination and clustering, guided by an information entropy metric. Extensive experimentation compares our method to existing techniques, yielding compelling results that support its efficacy and outperform existing approaches in accuracy and non-parametric statistical analysis. The code supporting our research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/InfoDrive/UAPS. This project has been approved by the university's Institutional Review Board (IRB-17-2782-1-F). The associated IRB approval can be accessed through the UAPS repository. The UAPS dataset, used in this research, can be obtained from the InfoDrive repository. This dataset comprises user-perceived web page structures collected through human participation in the study. The UAPS method has practical applications in enhancing the visual web page structure and supporting search operations, as demonstrated in the previous studies. Recently, visual search and web-search research have shown promising development, spurred by the emerging semantic web technologies and the availability of large datasets. Nonetheless, the existing research has yet to provide a comprehensive user-perceived web page structure. This has been attributed to the inherent difficulties in manually reorganizing the dynamic web pages. Our research targets this issue by presenting a new method that provides the user-perceived web page structure, while addressing the core challenges involved. The approach is evaluated based on its precision and fidelity using the UAPS dataset, comprising real user-perceived web page structures. The results show that our method surpasses the current state-of-the-art techniques in both metrics. Furthermore, the results suggest that our method is efficient as it can process over 90% of the uAPS pages within 5 seconds of computational time. The algorithm's efficacy has been supported by both empirical analysis and statistical testing without any significant deviations. The algorithm's theoretical foundations reveal that its maximal attainment is 1, meaning it can provide a perfect user-perceived web page structure when the input rank-limited pages are at most 1. This is further validated by the results of the rank-limited uAPS dataset, where our method outperforms the existing approaches in both precision and fidelity when the rank is at most 3.

A specific number $N$ is considered ''friendly'' if there is a pair $(p,q)$ of distinct prime numbers such that $p\cdot q=N$ and $||p||=|q|$. This investigation seeks to determine the primes $p$ and $q$ in $N=130=N_{109}\cdot N_{21}$ where $109$ and $21$ are prime numbers. 

  In general, for a product number $N$ with its prime factorization $p_1^{k_1}\cdots p_{\lambda(N)}^{k_1}$, the set $\mathcal{P}(N)$, known as the prime factorization set, is defined as the collection of exponents $(k_1,\ldots,k_{\lambda(N)})$ where $1\le i\le\lambda(N)$. In this case, the prime factorizations of $109$ and $21$ are $109=109^{1}$ and $21=3\cdot 7$. 

  In order to identify the desired primes $p$ and $q$, we break down the problem into two distinct cases. In our first case, we look for a prime $p$ equal to $109$, and then determine the prime factorization of $N/109=15=3\cdot 5$. In our second case, we find the prime $q=21$, and examine the prime factorization of $N/21=5=5^{1}$. 

  In this investigation, we provide a straightforward method to identify the desired primes $p$ and $q$ in any friendly number $N$ based on its prime factorizations, and also offer an efficient approach to compute $\mathcal{P}(N)$. A novelly designed computer program is used to identify the prime numbers satisfying the conditions defined by the first two cases. In our analysis, we discuss the third case where $N$ is equal to $109\cdot 21=2349$ and identify the prime numbers satisfying the conditions. Additionally, we explain the requirements for avoiding infinite loops in the case where $N$ is equal to the product of two prime numbers, $p$ and $q$, and provide a method to identify the prime numbers satisfying the conditions in any such number $N$.

  We began by examining how the cluster's bound fraction, average temperature, and size change in response to changes in the core and envelope structures. 

  We analyzed three distinct cluster structures - homogeneous, radial, and hierarchical - and found that a homogeneous core and isothermal envelope produces a cluster with a globally radial structure, while a hierarchical core and isothermal envelope results in a cluster with two distinct temperature zones. 

  We also discovered that a cluster with a Makkai-Zhang core and an isothermal envelope exhibits global properties similar to a radial cluster, with two temperature zones emerging only at higher tidal radii and radial mass concentrations. 

  However, a radial mass distribution can arise from a combination of two distinct core structures, either a compact Makkai-Zhang core or a broader Gaussian core, provided the latter has a low average radius. 

  We further explored how these cluster structures were affected by changes in the tidal radii and found that a transition from a single to a dual-temperature structure can occur across a broad range of tidal radii, but also that a mass-concentration structure can develop only at lower tidal radii. 

  We finally observed that a hierarchical core can give way to a mass-concentration structure, while a Makkai-Zhang or Gaussian core requires a specific low value to create such a structure, with two temperature structures emerging from a hierarchical core at higher tidal radii and a Makkai-Zhang or Gaussian core at lower tidal radii. 

  These predictions from our model suggest that a mass-concentration structure is more likely to occur at higher metallicity, a theory supported by the data, with such concentrations more prevalent in richer regions of the galaxy. 

  We also create a diagram showing the dependence of the cluster structure on the binding energy and metallicity, with the range of possible structures, including mass-concentration, two temperature, and homogenous structures clearly illustrated. 

  This model's success in creating a mass-concentration structure, a phenomenon observed in many star clusters, is further reinforced by the agreement with established observations of these clusters. 

  We also note that a mass-concentration structure can give way to a two temperature structure at higher velocities and a hierarchical core structure at higher velocities and richer metals, with such effects evident in the cluster structure at higher velocities and richer metals, a phenomenon that is not however, the primary subject of this study.

Using tools from Fairness literature, we show that social distancing policies can be viewed as a classification system that separates individuals into high and low-risk groups to impose distance measures on specific populations. Next, we develop a framework to evaluate the balance of risk between different groups under various distancing schemes. This framework enables various types of distancing interventions, such as targeted school closures and stay-at-home orders, to be assessed based on their impact on vulnerable populations. Through this approach, decision-makers can critically examine different distancing strategies and their effects on different groups, ultimately choosing a plan that minimizes human suffering and infection rates. To illustrate the value of our framework, we study a simple SIR model, where we apply it to the United States and Arkansas to evaluate the generalizability of our methods. Ultimately, decision-makers face a difficult task: they must weigh the need to reduce infection rates against the potential human costs of stricter distancing measures and the difficult ethical choices that come with them. By providing a framework to examine these ethics more closely, we can make distancing policies more just and potentially reduce some of the social and economic consequences associated with them. Numerical calculations in our research show that, in many cases, "non-pharmaceutical interventions" can significantly reduce infection rates, and the impact of these measures can be particularly pronounced when they are targeted at schools and larger public gatherings. The results of our research suggest that, if we can accurately identify at-risk groups and the government can effectively implement distancing measures, we can reduce infection rates by up to 50% and even increase the overall well-being of vulnerable groups. The value of our framework lies in its ability to help decision-makers make informed decisions about the effectiveness and ethics of different distancing strategies, even those that seem small, like school closures. By applying our methods, decision-makers can examine the impact of these interventions, reduce virus spread, and make distancing policies more just and fair. The long-term potential of our research is to contribute to better pandemic management by providing decision-makers with a more informed perspective on the various distancing strategies available to them. The idea is that even slight changes in distancing policies can have different effects on various groups and that it is our responsibility to make those who are most vulnerable to infection also the primary focus of our protection. A particular challenge for these methods is the growing concern over their environmental impact, leading to a desire to reduce their carbon footprint while maintaining their performance. Our study involves comparing the predictive capabilities of both types of models on a sentiment analysis task on a specific dataset, with a particular focus on assessing their climate impact using the Carbon Impact tool. The results show that both models achieve comparable accuracy, but the Transformer-based model exhibits significantly lower climate impact. To address this, a new question was explored: Can MLP models be optimized to reduce their climate impact without sacrificing their performance? Our study provides a positive answer, presenting an optimization approach that not only decreases the climate impact of MLPs to near-transformer levels but also improves their overall prediction accuracy. A key aspect of this approach involves utilizing an existing dataset to fine-tune the model, highlighting the climate-saving potential of transfer learning techniques. Our findings indicate that transfer learning can reduce the climate impact of MLPs by approximately 80%, with no adverse effect on their accuracy. This optimization process can be applied to various text analysis tasks, offering a significant climate benefit while enhancing performance. Our research further approximates an upper limit for the climate impact that MLPs can reach, known as their climate bottleneck. This discovery opens up new possibilities for future research, suggesting that complex neural network models could be optimized to reach the climate bottleneck of transformed models on certain tasks. Our study provides valuable insights, contributing to the growing conversation around the climate impact of AI models. One of these logic units, the majority voter, can perform tasks that traditional arithmetic logic units cannot, like multiplying numbers larger than 1. This demonstration of new logic capabilities contributes to building a more comprehensive logic foundation for neuromorphic technology development. In addition to the majority voter, we also analyze another logical element, the minority voter, and its connection to the majority voter. Both logic elements are built using a single type of memristive device that can switch between two resistance states. This includes a realization of a 4-bit majority voter in an integrated circuit with four input ports. All computations are done on the basis of resistances in a circuit, eliminating the need for active elements like transistors. This makes the integration of these memristive logic elements into CMOS integrated circuits more straightforward. To back up our claims, we also model the microelectronic circuit designs of the majority voter and its CMOS integrated circuit, including a demonstration of the first supply-independent majority voter. This circuit can operate reliably in the presence of varying power supply voltages because of its dynamic threshold logic. This type of logic can function on any microelectronic circuit that can process the four resistance states of the memristive devices. Last but not least, we also simulate a neuromorphic computing architecture based on the majority voter, combining it with spiking neural networks to solve complex computational tasks. To ensure a seamless and efficient data transfer process, it is necessary to dynamically adjust network settings according to changing system conditions. Such adjustments can be achieved through sleep scheduling, where specific network devices temporarily disable their transmission receivers, resulting in reduced interference for other devices in the network and thus facilitating a more optimal data transfer process. This study proposes a sleep scheduling protocol for IoT networks based on partial overlay technology and IEEE 802.15.2 standard requirements, allowing for the synchronization of local area network layers and frequency bands. The proposed protocol enables a certain node to transition between active and sleep states according to a predetermined schedule, where the network remains operational and data transfer occurs between remaining nodes. To further optimize the sleep scheduling strategy, we developed a check-and-change mechanism that enables a specific node to stay awake if its transition to a sleep state would negatively affect other connected devices. By applying this mechanism, the overall network performance can be improved. The efficacy of the proposed protocol was tested by comparing it to existing strategies, where simulations showed that it outperforms these strategies by achieving an average packet delivery ratio of around 99% and an average end-to-end delay of around 150ms. Furthermore, the results showed that the sleep scheduling protocol can result in a reduction of power consumption of around 30% while maintaining an acceptable network performance. This study's findings are valid for various network conditions, including different node speeds and channel conditions. The optimal performance was achieved when the sleep scheduling strategy was applied for a duration of around 250ms and repeated around 400 times per second. Future developments of this work could involve expanding the protocol to other network layers and exploring the use of sleep scheduling in other types of wireless networks. Additionally, it is possible to utilize other types of data transfer technologies, such as duty cycling, in place of sleep scheduling. However, the specific technique used should result in a more optimal trade-off between network performance and energy consumption. Finally, it is essential to note that the performance of this protocol may degrade in the presence of hidden terminals, where data transfer may result in successful reception indications but actual data corruption. Therefore, it is necessary to employ additional error-detection mechanisms to further optimize the sleep scheduling strategy and other network layers. The use of such methods could lead to a more resilient data transfer process and improved overall network performance. The current study's work has been in development for the past two years and was inspired by observing the need for more efficient sleep scheduling strategies in wireless

This goal is critical for developing effective cross-institution person re-ID methods, which can match identified individuals across different surveillance systems without prior knowledge of their associations. Unfortunately, current unsupervised re-ID methods exhibit limited cross-institution generalization capabilities due to their reliance on pairwise similarity calculations and lack of label-aware training techniques. This paper addresses these challenges by employing a supervised model trained with labels on one dataset to improve its performance on another dataset without labels. Our approach involves contrastive training, hard sample mining, and incorporating a feature normalization module to enhance its effectiveness. Moreover, we introduce a metric learning objective and a regularization term to restrict the learned feature space, and propose ChAMP, a computational framework to evaluate cross-institution re-ID without labeled data inputs. Experiments on six datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method over other unsupervised re-ID methods, and we release our source code at https://github.com/jaykim98/CEAL.

a rapidly developing field of study, yet nearly all research has overlooked its practical implications in the social dynamics of communities of color. Due to historical and ongoing racial injustices, such as police brutality, people of color may be justified in their concern that their racial and ethnic backgrounds make them more recognizable as threats. This study investigates how visual cues like race, gender, and attire influence perceived threat identification in crowds, particularly in the context of a male shooter. Using a large dataset of images featuring human figures in various poses, backgrounds, and facial expressions, we examine how visual features impact perceived danger. Our analysis reveals that race significantly impacts perceived danger, with white individuals being less frequently identified as threats compared to people of color. Furthermore, we find that gender and attire also contribute to variations in threat identification. These findings show that deep neural network-based vision models like Fast-Shot are not immune to the societal biases and injustices inherent in the data from which they were developed. Ultimately, we hope that our study sparks meaningful discussions and applications within the machine learning community to mitigate the harmful biases inherent in machine-based visual identification systems. The knowledge gained from our research can also inform human experts in the social and psychological underpinnings of racial bias and injustice. The code and dataset for this study are available on GitHub for further research and replication. \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\
